picks.title: Explain a Bar Graph
picks.skill: Describing data in writing
picks.skillEs: describir datos por escrito
picks.directions: Imagine a class survey. Write 3-4 sentences that explain what the data shows. Use comparison words.
picks.prompt: The cafeteria manager wants to know which lunch to serve more often. Our class voted: pizza got 14 votes, tacos got 9, and salad got 4. Write 3-4 sentences that explain what the data shows.

vocab.meaning: facts or numbers you collect
to show how things differ
chosen by many people

models.A: Pizza got the most votes. Salad got the least. More students chose pizza than tacos.
models.B: The data shows that pizza is the most popular lunch with 14 votes. More students chose pizza than tacos, which got 9 votes. The least popular was salad with 4 votes.
models.C: The data shows that pizza is the clear favorite, with 14 of the 27 votes. Tacos came second with 9 votes, which is 5 fewer than pizza. Salad was the least popular with only 4 votes. The cafeteria should serve pizza more often, but it could also ask why so few students chose salad.

sayFor: the most and least popular choices
what the data means for the cafeteria
picks.hint: Use words like "most," "fewer than," and "the least" to compare the numbers.
picks.extension: Predict what might change if the class voted again next month.

picks.title: Summarize a Short Text
picks.skill: Writing a brief summary
picks.skillEs: escribir un resumen breve
picks.directions: Read the short text in your head, then write a 3-4 sentence summary in your own words.
picks.prompt: Your class newsletter has room for a short summary about recycling. Summarize this text in 3-4 sentences in your own words: "Recycling turns used items into new products. It saves energy and keeps trash out of landfills. Many cities now collect paper, plastic, and glass at the curb."

vocab.meaning: a short retelling of the main points
making used items into new ones
a place where trash is buried

models.A: This text is about recycling. It saves energy. Cities collect it.
models.B: This text is mainly about recycling. According to the text, recycling makes new products from old ones and saves energy. It also keeps trash out of landfills.
models.C: This text is mainly about how recycling helps the environment. According to the text, used paper, plastic, and glass can be turned into new products. This saves energy and means less trash ends up in landfills. In summary, recycling is easier than ever because many cities pick it up at the curb.

sayFor: the main idea in one sentence
picks.hint: A summary states the main idea first, then one or two key details. Do not copy the text exactly.
picks.extension: Add one opinion sentence telling whether you think recycling is worth it.

picks.title: Write: Compare Two Choices
picks.skill: Writing a comparison with transition words
picks.skillEs: escribir una comparación con palabras de transición
picks.directions: Compare two after-school activities. Write 4–6 sentences. Tell how they are alike and different, then choose one.
picks.prompt: Your younger cousin is choosing an after-school activity and asks for your advice. Compare joining the soccer team and joining the art club. How are they alike and different? Which would you choose, and why?

vocab.meaning: tell how things are alike
tell how things are different
a word that shows a difference

models.A: Both are after school. Soccer is outside, but art is inside. I would choose art because I like to draw.
models.B: Both soccer and art club are fun ways to meet friends. However, soccer is outside and active, while art club is quiet and creative. I would choose soccer because I like to run.
models.C: Both the soccer team and the art club meet after school, and both are good ways to make friends. However, soccer players practice outside and need to be fit, while art club members work indoors with paint and clay. On the other hand, art club meets only once a week, so it is easier to fit with homework. I would choose the art club because I want to improve my drawing and still have time to study.

picks.hint: Start with one similarity, then two differences, then your choice.
picks.extension: Add one sentence about who would enjoy each activity.

picks.title: Write: Explain with Evidence
picks.skill: Writing an explanation supported by evidence
picks.skillEs: escribir una explicación apoyada con evidencia
picks.directions: Write 4–6 connected sentences. Make a claim and support it with evidence using 'because,' 'but,' and 'so.'
picks.prompt: The principal is deciding whether to start a garden club and wants student input. Should our school start a garden club? Make a claim and support it with at least two reasons.

vocab.meaning: a statement you support
facts that support a claim
a word that shows contrast

models.A: Our school should start a garden club because it is fun. For example, we can grow food. Some people think it is hard, but we can learn. So we should do it.
models.B: Our school should start a garden club because students can learn science outside. For example, we could measure how fast tomato plants grow. Some people think it costs too much, but seeds are cheap. So a garden club is a good idea.
models.C: Our school should start a garden club because it would turn science lessons into real experiences. For example, students could test which soil helps beans grow fastest and record the data each week. The vegetables could also go to the cafeteria salad bar, so students would eat healthier food. Some people think a garden needs too much care in summer, but families could sign up to water it one week each. So a garden club would help students learn, eat better, and work together.

picks.hint: Claim → reason → example → address an objection → conclusion.
picks.extension: Add a specific number or fact as evidence.

picks.title: Write: Persuade Your Principal
picks.skill: Writing a short persuasive message to an audience
picks.skillEs: escribir un mensaje corto para convencer a un público
picks.directions: Write a short message (5–6 sentences) to persuade the principal. State your request, give two reasons, and end politely.
picks.prompt: Write to your principal asking for more time in the library each week. Give two reasons and a polite ending.
frames: Dear Principal ___, I am writing because ___.

vocab.meaning: to convince someone to agree
something you politely ask for
polite and considerate

models.A: Dear Principal Gómez, I want more library time. First, I like books. Second, I can study. Thank you.
models.B: Dear Principal Gómez, I am writing because I would like more time in the library each week. First, we need time to find books for our reading logs. Second, the library has computers for research projects. Thank you for thinking about our request.
models.C: Dear Principal Gómez, I am writing because our class would like one more library period each week. First, we have only 20 minutes now, which is not enough time to choose a book and start reading. Second, we have a research project this month, and the library has the computers we need. If a full period is not possible, even 15 extra minutes would help. Thank you for considering our request. Sincerely, Room 214

picks.hint: Greeting → request → reason 1 → reason 2 → polite closing.
picks.extension: Add a sentence that answers a possible 'no' from the principal.

picks.title: Explain: Why Do We Have Seasons?
picks.skill: Writing an explanatory paragraph from a diagram
picks.skillEs: escribir un párrafo explicativo a partir de un diagrama
picks.directions: Look at the diagram of Earth orbiting the Sun. Write an explanatory paragraph (5-7 sentences) that explains why the Northern Hemisphere has summer and winter.
picks.prompt: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer in June and winter in December. Use the diagram and precise science vocabulary.

picture.alt: A diagram of the Sun in the center with Earth shown at two places in its orbit. On the left, Earth's tilted axis leans its northern half toward the Sun, and sunlight hits the north directly. On the right, on the opposite side of the orbit, the same tilt now leans the northern half away from the Sun, and sunlight hits the north at a low slant.

frames: In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted ___, so ___.

vocab.meaning: an imaginary line that Earth spins around
the path a planet travels around the Sun
one half of Earth

models.A: Earth is tilted. In June, the top of Earth leans toward the Sun. It gets more sunlight, so it is summer. In December, it leans away, so it is winter.
models.B: We have seasons because Earth is tilted. In June, the top of Earth leans toward the Sun, so it gets more sunlight and it is summer. In December, the top of Earth leans away from the Sun, so it gets less sunlight and it is winter. The tilt stays the same all year.
models.C: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer. As a result, the ground and air absorb more energy, and it is summer. Six months later, in December, Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. Sunlight hits it at a low angle and spreads out, and days are shorter, so it is winter. Many people think seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun, but it is actually the tilt that matters.

sayFor: a topic sentence that names the cause (Earth's tilt)
a concluding sentence that corrects a common mistake
picks.hint: Distance is NOT the reason for seasons. Focus on the tilt: which half leans toward the Sun in each month?
picks.extension: Add a sentence explaining what season Australia has in June, and why.

picks.title: Phones at Lunch: Make an Argument
picks.skill: Writing a claim with evidence
picks.skillEs: escribir una afirmación con evidencia
picks.directions: Write a short paragraph (4-6 sentences) that states a claim and supports it with two reasons.
picks.prompt: The principal is considering a new phone rule for lunch and invited students to write to her. Should students be allowed to use phones during lunch? State your claim and support it with two reasons.

vocab.meaning: the position you argue for
why your claim is true
the sentence that wraps up your idea

models.A: I believe phones should be allowed at lunch. One reason is we can call family. Another reason is we can relax. Therefore, phones are okay at lunch.
models.B: I believe students should not use phones during lunch. One reason is that lunch is the only time to talk with friends face to face. Another reason is that phones slow down the line because students do not pay attention. Therefore, phones should stay in backpacks during lunch.
models.C: I believe students should not be allowed to use phones during lunch. One reason is that lunch is one of the few times in the day when students can talk face to face; for example, in my cafeteria, tables where phones are out are often silent. Another reason is that phones cause conflicts, such as students taking photos of others without asking. On the other hand, some families want to reach their children, but students can use the office phone in an emergency. In conclusion, a phone-free lunch would help students build real friendships and feel safer.

sayFor: two reasons, at least one with an example
a conclusion that restates your claim
picks.hint: Start with your claim, give two reasons, add an example, and finish with a conclusion sentence.
picks.extension: Add one sentence that answers a person who disagrees with you.

picks.title: Bus or Walking: Compare Ways to School
picks.skill: Writing a compare-and-contrast response
picks.skillEs: escribir una respuesta que compare y contraste
picks.directions: Write a paragraph comparing two ways to get to school. Explain which is better and why.
picks.prompt: The school's family newsletter is writing about ways to get to school. Compare riding the bus and walking to school. Which is better and why? Write 4-6 sentences.

vocab.meaning: to show how things are alike
to show how things are different
considering everything together

models.A: Both the bus and walking get you to school. The bus is fast, but walking is healthy. Walking is also free. Overall, walking is better.
models.B: Both riding the bus and walking get students to school on time. However, the bus is faster when you live far away, while walking gives you exercise. Walking also does not depend on a schedule. Overall, walking is better because it is healthy and free.
models.C: Both riding the bus and walking get students to school on time, and both let them travel with friends. However, the bus is faster and safer for students who live more than a mile away, especially in bad weather. In contrast, walking gives students exercise and fresh air before class, and it does not depend on a bus schedule. Walking can also be safe when students travel in groups and use crosswalks. Overall, walking is the better choice for students who live close to school, but the bus is smarter for long distances.

picks.hint: Show one way they are alike and two ways they are different, then state which is better.
picks.extension: Add a sentence about which choice is better in bad weather.

picks.title: Write a Narrative: When the Lights Went Out
picks.skill: Developing a narrative with sequence, dialogue, and detail
picks.skillEs: desarrollar una narración con orden, diálogo y detalles
picks.directions: Read the opening of a story. Then continue the story in your own words.
picks.prompt: Opening: "When the lights went out in the middle of the school play, Ana froze on stage." Write 7-9 sentences that continue the story. Show what happens next in order, include one line of dialogue, describe what Ana sees, hears, or feels, and end by showing how the problem was solved.

vocab.meaning: words that characters say, written inside quotation marks
the order in which events happen
the way the problem in a story is solved

models.A: Ana froze on the stage. It was dark. She heard people talking. Her friend said, "Keep going." Ana said her lines. The lights came on, and everyone clapped.
models.B: When the lights went out, Ana froze on stage. She heard the audience whisper in the dark. Then her friend Leo whispered, "Keep going, you know your lines." Ana took a deep breath and spoke. A few seconds later, the lights came back on, and everyone clapped. Ana felt proud.
models.C: The dark stage suddenly felt enormous, and Ana could hear the audience murmuring and chairs creaking. Her heart pounded so loudly that she forgot her next line. At that moment, her friend Leo leaned close and whispered, "Just say it the way we practiced." Ana closed her eyes, took a slow breath, and began to speak, her voice shaking at first and then growing steadier. A few seconds later, the lights flickered back on, and the audience burst into applause. Although her hands were still trembling, Ana smiled, because she had learned that she could keep going even when everything went wrong.

sayFor: events in a clear order with time words
one line of dialogue with quotation marks
details about what Ana sees, hears, or feels
a closing sentence that shows what Ana learned
picks.hint: Plan the moment in three parts: what Ana feels, who helps her, and how the lights come back. Add one sound and one feeling.
picks.extension: Add a sentence at the end that tells how Ana acts differently the next time something goes wrong.

picks.title: Compare and Contrast: Athens and Sparta
picks.skill: Writing a compare-and-contrast paragraph from a table
picks.skillEs: escribir un párrafo que compare y contraste a partir de una tabla
picks.directions: Both Athens and Sparta were city-states in ancient Greece. Use the information in the table to write a compare-and-contrast paragraph.
picks.prompt: Write a paragraph of 6-8 sentences about how Athens and Sparta were alike and how they were different. Compare at least two topics from the table, and end with a sentence that explains what the differences show.

vocab.meaning: a city with its own government and land
a person who has rights and duties in a city or country
strict training and self-control

models.A: Athens and Sparta were both Greek cities. In Athens, men voted. In Sparta, kings led the city. Boys in Sparta trained to be soldiers.
models.B: Athens and Sparta were both city-states in ancient Greece, but they were different. In Athens, male citizens voted on laws, but in Sparta two kings led the city. Boys in Athens studied music and public speaking. Boys in Sparta left home at age 7 to train as soldiers.
models.C: Athens and Sparta were both powerful city-states in ancient Greece, yet they valued very different things. In Athens, male citizens voted on laws in an assembly, whereas Sparta was led by two kings and a small council. Both cities educated boys, but the goals were not the same: many Athenian boys studied reading, music, and public speaking, while Spartan boys left home at age 7 to train as soldiers. Unlike Athens, which honored art, philosophy, and trade, Sparta treated discipline and military strength as most important. These differences show that two cities in the same civilization can build very different ways of life.

sayFor: a topic sentence that introduces both city-states
at least two topics compared, such as government, education, or values
comparison words (both, similarly, whereas, in contrast)
a concluding sentence about what the differences show
picks.hint: Read across each row of the table so you compare the SAME topic for both cities before you move on to the next topic.
picks.extension: Add a sentence that predicts how a Spartan boy and an Athenian boy might each describe a good citizen.
